Deep foundation (piles or well foundation)
Water can scour and undermine the ground beneath a shallow foundation – one of the classic reasons for a deep foundation (e.g. bridge piers in a river).
With a strongly inclined load, a shallow foundation could slide; piles also take the horizontal force.
Mixed foundation: piled raft
There is no better layer deeper down, but the load of the tower block is large: the raft alone would settle too much, and the piles reduce it.
Raft foundation – the load spread over a large area
The near-surface layer is not very strong, but there is nothing better deeper down: the weight of the building has to be spread over a large area.
For a superstructure sensitive to settlement, a stiff raft also reduces the differential settlements.
The bearing stratum starts at a depth of ${fmt(st.tb, 1)} m – it is close to the surface.

Pad foundations (block footings with pocket necks)
For a hall sensitive to settlement, the differential settlement between the columns has to be reduced in both directions.
The load of the tower block is large and concentrated: it has to be transferred over the full plan area.
Raft foundation on the weaker layer (without groundwater lowering)
The bearing stratum (${fmt(st.tb, 1)} m) is below the groundwater: a deepened foundation would need dewatering.
The structure is not sensitive to settlement, so a near-surface raft avoids costly dewatering or deep foundations.
Deep foundation (piles) – because of the high groundwater
The bearing stratum is below the groundwater: the high groundwater level during construction makes a shallow foundation more expensive.
Because of the large loads, it is worth using the bearing resistance of the deeper layer with piles.
Mixed foundation or piles
The large load of the tower block can be carried by the deeper bearing stratum; the raft and piles acting together are the economical choice.
Deepened shallow foundation on the bearing stratum
The bearing stratum is ${fmt(st.tb, 1)} m deep, but the groundwater stays below it: down to 3–5 m the shallow-foundation technique still works.
Its bearing resistance is calculated as for a shallow foundation, neglecting the shaft resistance.
Raft foundation on the weaker layer – if the settlement is tolerable
The reliable bearing stratum is only at ${fmt(st.tb, 1)} m depth.
If the structure is not sensitive, a near-surface raft avoids a deep foundation – but this has to be verified with a settlement calculation.

Fixed connection: the main bars (starter bars) of the column are anchored down into the footing, so the joint also transfers moment. The footing has at least a mesh of reinforcement at the bottom.
Pinned connection: the column narrows at the joint, the gap is filled with a flexible material, and the bars transfer the shear and the vertical force – practically no moment.
Earlier solution: precast reinforced concrete pocket foundation. The column was set into the “pocket” of the footing and then fixed in its final position by concreting it in.
Today’s solution: the precast column is set and fixed in a pocket neck placed on a cast-in-place reinforced concrete block (or slab).
Steel column on a concrete footing: base plate, grout and holding-down bolts. The bolted connection is needed to transfer any tensile forces (a moment-resisting connection in one or two directions).
Structure with a closed plan (water tower, factory chimney): a footing built as a single block, usually circular in plan – essentially a large pad foundation.

Flat slab of constant thickness: for relatively small loads. Simple to form and reinforce, but flexible.
Raft with upstand ribs: ribs standing up along the walls and columns stiffen it. The underside stays flat, and the spaces between the ribs are filled.
Raft with downstand ribs: the ribs reach into the ground. The top gives a flat floor, but trenches have to be dug for the ribs.
“Flat-slab” (mushroom) type raft: in framed buildings with larger loads, thickening under the columns prevents punching.
Raft with hidden ribs: only additional reinforcement remains where the ribs would be, and the thickness equals that of the ribs.

Ground-bearing raft: only the topsoil and (part of) the made ground are removed; the reinforced slab is placed on a well-compacted granular bedding layer at least 50–60 cm thick, and its underside stays (may stay) above the frost depth. It can be used for buildings of a few storeys, on less favourable ground and with high groundwater too.

Two-storey masonry family house. The sandy gravel bearing stratum starts at 1.1 m depth, and the groundwater is deep.

Masonry building, good ground near the surface: strip footings under the walls are the simplest and cheapest.
Steel-framed industrial hall with a 6 m column spacing, on good granular soil. Differential settlement between the columns causes no problem.
good granular soil
Concentrated column loads, settlements that can be treated separately: pad foundations (with holding-down bolts for a steel column, with a pocket neck for a precast column).
A row of columns on weaker ground: unacceptably large differential settlement would develop between the columns in one direction.
weaker ground
The continuous beam foundation (ground beam) ties the row of columns in one direction and gives longitudinal stiffness.
A square column grid where the differential settlements have to be reduced in both directions, but the full plan area is not yet needed.
Intersecting ground beams: a beam-grid foundation.
A 10-storey block of flats with a full basement; the design groundwater level is above the basement floor, and separate footings would almost touch each other.
high groundwater
The load has to be transferred over the full plan area, and because of the high groundwater a watertight reinforced concrete slab (“inverted floor”) is needed: a raft foundation.
A panel building of prefabricated elements, which can tolerate only very small deformations without damage.
tolerates small deformation
The box girder of the base slab, basement walls and floor acting together – the box foundation – gives the necessary stiffness.
A water tower with a closed, circular plan; the whole load reaches the ground through a single concentrated block.
circular plan
The footings of structures with a closed plan, built as a single block and usually circular in plan, are essentially large pad foundations.
Two-storey building on weak but not organic near-surface ground with high groundwater; the made ground is partly removed, and compacted granular bedding is built.
